newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Another Seoul banker arrested on bribery charges.
newsitem.headline: Another Seoul banker arrested on bribery charges.

text.p: The head of a leading South Korean bank was arrested on Saturday in the latest of a string of corruption scandals involving 14 other bankers.
State prosecutors said they put Sohn Hong-gyun, president of SEOULBANK, behind bars on bribery charges. SEOULBANK is South Korea's sixth largest bank in terms of deposits.
Sohn is charged with accepting 100 million won ($121,000) on four occasions last year in return for providing loans to a local valve-making company, a prosecution spokesman said.

He is the latest prominent figure in South Korea to be hit by an anti-corruption drive spearheaded by President Kim Young-sam, in which hundreds of senior civil servants, bankers and businessmen have been arrested.
The prosecution spokesman accused Sohn of "arranging loans in excess of the legal limits" in return for bribes from the valve manufacturer. The head of the company is being probed.
"We will interview other SEOULBANK executives and trace Sohn's bank accounts to find out if there were other irregularities," a senior prosecutor told reorters.

He said Sohn accepted bank accounts under the name of the valve company's executive and registered seals to cover up illegal deals. Banks use registered seals in South Korea as well as signatures to authorise transactions.
Fourteen other bank heads have been arrested or sacked for involvement in corruption scandals since President Kim took office in 1993.

In August, Rhee Chul-soo, ex-president of Korea First Bank, was sentenced to three years in jail after being found guilty of accepting 280 million won in return for approving millions of dollars worth of loans to two local companies.
"Banks are priority target for purge," said the newspaper Dong-A Ilbo, referring to rampant kickbacks involved in seeking bank loans.
"Scarce funds and high interest rates in unofficial money markets mean getting a loan is a privilege in South Korea," a banking analyst at brokerage Daewoo Securities said.

Analysts said local banks, which provided cheap loans to the country's industrial sector under government policies for rapid modernisation in the 1970s amd 1980s, were not competitive against foreign banks either.
"Commissions are given to bank officials to maintain close relationships (to ensure a loan) and this led to many bad loans being piled up," one local analyst said.
At the end of last year 25 local commercial banks had a combined total of 2.29 trillion won in bad loans, up 19 percent from a year earlier, a Hyundai Securities report said.

The succession of scandals has embarrassed Kim, who has staked his reputation as an anti-corruption campaigner. His drive to clean up South Korean society has brought to justice former presidents Roh Tae-woo and Chun Doo Hwan.
Roh is appealing a 22-1/2 year jail sentence imposed for bribery, treason and mutiny. His predecessor, Chun, is appealing a death sentence on similar convictions.
Last month, Kim dismissed his defence minister, Lee Yang-ho, who was charged last week with accepting bribes and leaking secrets in connection with arms procurement.
Kim's health minister, Lee Sung-ho, stepped down last week amid bribery allegations involving his wife. He was cleared of any wrongdoing but his wife was charged with bribery.
